candidate.blueprint_locator: Client Needs category 'Basic Care and Comfort' — nursing care that assists with activities of daily living and comfort; applied here to elimination/ostomy self-care and skin protection.
candidate.educational_objective: Manage peristomal irritant skin injury from stool leakage by promptly changing the leaking pouching system, assessing the skin and barrier fit, and ensuring a close-fitting barrier opening rather than patching the leak.

options.A: Gently cleanse the peristomal skin, reassess the pouching-system fit so the barrier opening fits closely around the stoma, and replace the leaking system rather than taping over the leak.
options.B: Reapply the leaking pouch and reinforce the edges with additional tape so the appliance can remain in place despite the leak.
options.C: Cut the new barrier opening substantially larger than the stoma so more peristomal skin remains exposed to the stool.
options.D: Ignore the skin beneath the barrier because persistent burning and leakage do not require assessment until the next routine pouch change.

candidate.rationale: A is correct. WOCN identifies stool undermining the skin barrier as a cause of peristomal moisture-associated irritant skin damage. Its clinician and consumer guides direct prompt pouch/barrier change when there is burning or leakage, assessment of the skin and adhesive side of the barrier, and sizing the barrier opening to fit closely around the stoma base. WOCN also explicitly states to change a leaking pouch rather than reinforce it with additional tape. B is incorrect because taping over a leak leaves the cause and skin exposure uncorrected. C is incorrect because an oversized opening exposes more peristomal skin to effluent rather than creating the close fit WOCN recommends. D is incorrect because burning and leakage are specific triggers for immediate pouch-system assessment and change.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Effluent leakage can cause peristomal irritant skin damage; burning or leakage warrants prompt pouch-system change and skin/barrier assessment; the barrier opening should fit closely around the stoma base; leaking pouches should be changed rather than reinforced with tape.
candidate.source_document_title: Peristomal Skin Assessment Guide for Clinicians; Peristomal Skin Assessment Guide for Consumers
candidate.source_locator: Clinician Guide — 'Peristomal Moisture Associated Skin Damage (PMASD – Irritant Dermatitis)': 'Manage Probable Contributing Factors: Poor Fit of Pouching System', 'Skin Barrier Opening', 'Assure Appropriate Frequency of Pouching System Change', and 'Patient Education'; Clinician Guide — 'Frequency of Pouching System Change': 'Change pouch when leaking; do not reinforce with additional tape.' Consumer Guide — 'Healthy Peristomal Skin' → 'Tips for Better Skin Care' → 'Check Barrier/Pouching System Fit' and 'Frequency of Pouching System Change'.
candidate.source_organization: Wound, Ostomy and Continence Nurses Society (WOCN)
candidate.stem: A client with a new colostomy reports burning under the skin barrier. The nurse removes the pouch and finds stool has leaked beneath the barrier and the peristomal skin is red and moist. Which action is most appropriate?
